extracted.intended_audience: NPR listeners, fans of Tina Fey, and aspiring comedy writers/performers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical standards for writing and performing comedy across improv, sketch, television (SNL/30 Rock), and political satire, as discussed in a Tina Fey interview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make statements, don't ask questions
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the rules of improv: make statements. Don't ask questions, and put the onus on the other person to come up with something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied broadly (Fey explicitly applies it to women too): initiate and give your scene partner material to react to rather than deferring or apologizing with questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enter a scene when someone needs you
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't enter a scene just because you have an idea or want to be in it; enter when someone needs you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch the scene and step in to fix a lull or respond to a reference — contributing as part of the group rather than stealing focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actively listen as the core improv technique
rubrics_metrics.description: What you're supposed to be thinking about is actively listening to that person because you truly don't know what the next thing is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use attentive listening to respond truthfully and avoid 'watching yourself act' — this keeps performances alive and reactive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribute to the group, don't hog scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv is a group mindset: you never just come in because that scene looks fun and I want to be in it too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make contributions that help the ensemble; be willing to hold back until your entry benefits the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use improv process to create sketches (improv -> distill -> write)
rubrics_metrics.description: At Second City the process is to improvise, re-improvise and work together and then eventually write down the final version of what you improvised, which becomes a sketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop material collaboratively through performance, then capture the working version in writing for refinement and production.

rubrics_metrics.name: SNL procedural expectation: quick turnaround of pages
rubrics_metrics.description: At SNL you come in on Tuesday and by Wednesday morning you have to turn in about 20 pages of writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to produce large volumes on short deadlines; build material and improv-based bits that can be shaped quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: When writing for a host: ideas 'with type' and 'against type'
rubrics_metrics.description: Make two columns: a list of ideas that went with their type, and ideas that went strongly against type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitch both safe, host-appropriate bits and surprising, against-type concepts to give options and potentially get memorable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer/performer etiquette: if you're hired as a writer, don't perform unless needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If you were hired as a writer, that's not what you're there for; you usually shouldn't be a sketch performer unless necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect role boundaries in a writers' room and on a sketch show; appear only when production needs extra bodies or it's agreed upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer segments that 'look like you' for longevity (e.g., Update)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Weekend Update’ is the only segment in the show that is never cut; you look like a version of yourself and say your name weekly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct-address segments can build recognizability and are less vulnerable to being dropped; use them strategically in a televised career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust your instinct on sensitive topical humor
rubrics_metrics.description: After tragedies you must trust your own instinct as your guide: if this joke makes us feel queasy, it's probably not a good joke. And if it seems funny, it's probably funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the creators' gut reactions as a primary litmus test for appropriateness of topical jokes in difficult times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about explicit political endorsements in comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians are better used when they don't endorse; explicit endorsements can politicize and complicate a comedian's public role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid turning satire into overt political endorsement if you want to preserve comedic flexibility and avoid being perceived as a mouthpiece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of portrayal and awareness of perceived point-of-view
rubrics_metrics.description: If you portray a political figure frequently, pieces may be assumed to be your personal point of view; be mindful of that and try to manage control when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When doing recurring impersonations, consider how writing credit, authorship and context will shape audience interpretation and your own politicization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lasting two-shots with the real political figure
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that a two-shot with an impersonator and the real person can create an enduring image that outlives context (e.g., 'that's what they would play when I die').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about the long-term media artifacts you are creating; minimize images that will be replayed out of context if that concerns you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and intention determine acceptability of risky jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes are tricky because some of it is the context, and some of it is the intention of who's making the joke; you kind of don't know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate different readings, especially on race, gender, illness or disability; weigh whether intent and context will be understood by the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect performers' boundaries and personal circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing material that touches on a performer's personal life or health (e.g., Tracy Morgan's diabetes), be considerate of boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume collaborators may have limits; confirm comfort level, and be mindful when portraying real issues that affect someone's life.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-camera acting requires technical precision
rubrics_metrics.description: On film you must be physically precise: hit your mark so the lighting is right and stay out of each other's light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine improv mindset with film discipline — maintain active listening while meeting technical blocking and camera requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address representation and casting responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid defaulting to men-in-drag to play women when appropriate performers aren't available; seek authentic casting where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When casting gaps exist, acknowledge the limitation and prioritize finding performers of the right identity rather than relying on caricature or convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat the Internet as a forum worth engaging with
rubrics_metrics.description: The Internet is the repository of all human garbage; you should never respond to it (though Fey sometimes did in her book as a device).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid feeding trolls and anonymous nastiness; responding rarely improves anything and can escalate or distract from your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should not be presented as prescriptive exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters aren't showing you the right way to be at all; they're not prescriptive — at most they may spark discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft characters as complex, not moral lessons; accept that audiences may debate their meaning, and be prepared for misreadings.
